01 / INDUSTRY EXPERIENCE

work experience

AMAZON / SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT ENGINEER INTERN

150 → 45 hours

~70% reduction in representative investigation time.

For QueryQuencher, I built a TypeScript/AWS investigation workflow connecting an AI assistant to internal services through Model Context Protocol (MCP). Engineers previously had to trace information across 20+ tools and services; the workflow served a process with 300+ monthly users.

Audit responses ranged from ~100 KB to more than 10 MB. Loading full payloads into a model context or memory wasn't scalable, so I redesigned the retrieval flow around summary-first filtering, incremental processing, and deeper tool calls only when justified by the question. I worked through implementation, review, instrumentation, and validation as the design evolved.

What I worked on: context engineering · MCP tool boundaries · TypeScript · AWS · service integration · performance and failure handling

DEVELOPMENT FLOW / WHERE I ITERATED

Define investigation outcome → integrate services and MCP tools → prototype full-response retrieval → stress-test large audit payloads → redesign context and retrieval → review, observe, and validate

↺ The first approach hit memory, latency, and context limits. I went back from testing to data-access design: filter early, stream/incrementally handle results, and fetch detail only when necessary. A mid-internship overlap with another MCP effort also required a change in implementation direction.

01 / FULL-STACK APPLICATION

place memory

Find the real places in screenshots and notes you saved.

TRY THE DEMO ↗source ↗

FIELD NOTE / SAN FRANCISCO

one lake, two names

01 / THE PROBLEM
A screenshot said Stow Lake. The map said Blue Heron Lake. The first run needed manual confirmation.
02 / THE CHANGE
I added historical aliases to the evidence and filtered out candidates that weren’t the right kind of place.
03 / THE RESULT
The resolver identified Blue Heron Lake on the rerun and showed the alias behind the match.
read the field notes ↗

ARCHITECTURE & ENGINEERING DECISIONS

React/TypeScript UI → FastAPI API → Gemini multimodal clue extraction → Photon/OSM place search with Nominatim fallback → normalized candidate scoring and confidence checks → SQLite persistence. The public demo runs on Render.

The model supplies evidence, not a final place identity. Deterministic ranking, category filtering, source provenance, and a review/abstain path make incorrect automatic matches less likely. I split extraction, provider recall, and resolver accuracy into separate testable concerns; field failures informed alias support, retrieval fallback, and regression checks in CI.

Design tradeoff: This is tool-grounded retrieval, not embedding-based RAG. I kept SQLite and avoided Redis because the current traffic and latency haven't justified distributed caching. Evaluation prioritizes false automatic resolutions over simply maximizing coverage.

SDLC / FIELD-DRIVEN LOOPS

Define saved-place workflow → build UI/API/DB path → integrate Gemini and place providers → evaluate real artifacts → refine resolver and candidate retrieval → regression-test in CI → deploy and observe

↺ Generic notes led to an abstain rule; duplicate places led to deduplication; Stow Lake led to historical-name support and tighter alias parsing; upstream search failures led back to provider failover. Each loop changed the retrieval or decision boundary before returning to field tests.

02 / DATA ENGINEERING & ANALYTICS

immune cell population analysis

Reproducible clinical-trial cohort analysis, from validated cell counts to an interactive dashboard.

OPEN DASHBOARD ↗source ↗

ENGINEERING NOTE / COHORT ANALYSIS

from cell counts to defensible comparisons

01 / THE PROBLEM
Raw CSV rows describe multiple cell populations, samples, and subjects. Comparing response groups directly at the row level risks inconsistent counts and repeated-sample bias.
02 / THE DESIGN
Validate the input, normalize subject/sample/count relationships in SQLite, compute per-sample percentages, then aggregate repeated samples to the subject level before cohort statistics.
03 / THE RESULT
A three-tab Streamlit dashboard exposes sample frequencies, responder comparisons, and baseline subsets. In the supplied data, no population passed the adjusted FDR 0.05 threshold; the interface reports the tests without overstating significance.
read the methodology ↗

ARCHITECTURE & ENGINEERING DECISIONS

Supplied CSV → Python schema and consistency checks → SQLite subjects/samples/cell_counts tables → SQL frequencies and cohort queries → SciPy tests (Mann–Whitney U; Benjamini–Hochberg correction) → Streamlit/Plotly UI. The loaded dataset includes 3,500 subjects, 10,500 samples, and 52,500 count records.

Subject-level aggregation prevents repeated samples from being treated as independent participants. Input validation checks duplicate sample IDs, metadata consistency, and nonnegative integer counts. The repository documents a 27-test suite covering loading and analysis.

SDLC / DATA-VALIDATION LOOPS

Translate analytical questions → define CSV contract and relational schema → implement loader → derive SQL metrics → add cohort tests → present results in dashboard → verify calculations and edge cases

↺ Validation failures return to the input contract or loader, not to charts. Cohort-filter or repeated-sample discrepancies return to SQL and aggregation before statistical interpretation. Dashboard checks then loop back to the query and explanatory text to keep numbers auditable.

03 / MOBILE APPLICATION

eGym

Inclusive exercise planning around mobility, goals, equipment, and available time.

portfolio ↗

PRODUCT LOGIC & ACCESSIBILITY

Built a React Native/Expo prototype with onboarding and a questionnaire that selects exercises using explicit rules and user constraints. The application includes guided exercise flows and local session history. The important design choice was transparent, testable personalization rather than describing a rule-based system as AI-generated workouts.

SDLC / PROTOTYPE FEEDBACK LOOPS

Define inclusive exercise needs → design onboarding and questionnaire → implement exercise library and constraint-based picker → build routine and voice-guidance screens → save local sessions → manually walk through user flows

↺ Questionnaire answers feed back into routine selection: mobility, time, goals, and equipment change the candidate exercises. Mock login and AsyncStorage intentionally skip production authentication and backend infrastructure in this local prototype; those remain future development steps, not shipped features.
